materials.text:
Dragonboat guarantees the linearizability of your I/O when interacting with the
IStateMachine or IOnDiskStateMachine instances. In plain English, writes (via
making proposal) to your Raft cluster appears to be instantaneous, once a write
is completed, all later reads (linearizable read using the ReadIndex protocol
as implemented and provided in dragonboat) should return the value of that write
or a later write. Once a value is returned by a linearizable read, all later
reads should return the same value or the result of a later write.

To strictly provide such guarantee, we need to implement the at-most-once
semantic required by linearizability. For a client, when it retries the proposal
that failed to complete before its deadline during the previous attempt, it has
the risk to have the same proposal committed and applied twice into the user
state machine. Dragonboat prevents this by implementing the client session
concept described in Diego Ongaro's PhD thesis.

NodeHost instances across the network, this brings fault tolerance to machine
and network failures as application data stored in the Raft cluster will be
available as long as the majority of its managing NodeHost instances (i.e. its
underlying hosts) are available.

* It is recommended to use enterprise NVME SSD with high write endurance rating. Must use local hard disks and avoid any NFS, CIFS, Samba, CEPH or other similar shared storage.
* Never try to backup or restore Dragonboat data by directly operating on Dragonboat data files or directories. It can immediately corrupt your Raft clusters. 
* Each Raft group has multiple replicas, the best way to safeguard the availability of your services and data is to increase the number of replicas. As an example, the Raft group can tolerant 2 node failures when there are 5 replicas, while it can only tolerant 1 node failure when using 3 replicas. 
* On node failure, the Raft group will be available when it still has the quorum. To handle such failures, you can add an Observer node to start replicating data to it, once in sync with other replicas you can promote the Observer to a regular node and remove the failed node by using membership change APIs. For those failed nodes caused by intermittent failures such as short term network partition or power loss, you should resolve the network or power issue and try restarting the affected nodes.
* On disk failure, such as when experiencing data integrity check errors or write failures, it is important to immediately replace the failed disk and remove the failed node using the above described membership change method. To restart nodes with such disk failures, it is important to have the failed disk replaced first to ensure corrupted data is removed. As a refreshed node with no existing data, that node must be assigned a new RaftAddress value to avoid confusing other nodes. 
* When the quorum nodes are gone, you will not be able to resolve it without losing data. The github.com/lni/dragonboat/tools package provides the ImportSnapshot method to import a previously exported snapshot to repair such failed Raft cluster.
* By default, the RaftAddress value can not be changed between restarts, otherwise the system will panic with an error message.
* When you can't provide a static IP for your nodes, e.g. when IP is dynamically assigned on node restart, you may want to configure a static DNS name for that node and update it on each restart. 
* When it is not possible to do so, you can choose to set the AddressByNodeHostID field to enable the gossip feature which is designed to handle dynamic RaftAddress. Check godocs for more details on the gossip feature. 
* Always test your system to ensure that it has high availability by design, disaster recovery should always be a part of the CI.

feedback.answered:
Initial A1 backbone: the leader assigns term/index to proposals, records local replication progress, and computes a quorum order statistic over remotes and witnesses, excluding observers. tryCommit requires the selected entry to have the current term; followers check the preceding log term and bound commitment by the received suffix. Heartbeat commit is bounded by each recipient's match. ReadIndex separately requires a current-term committed entry for a multi-voter quorum, then gathers distinct heartbeat confirmations for a SystemCtx. Initial A2 backbone: campaigning increments term and records a self-vote; grants require available vote and an up-to-date log; Peer.Handle filters response senders against current participant maps before raft dispatch. Higher terms trigger state/reset transitions (subject to the documented recent-leader vote suppression); lower-term messages are ignored. Reset clears votes, pending readIndex state, transfer state and replication progress, while log commitment persists. New leadership appends a current-term no-op and reconstructs pending configuration-change status from the log. Election is blocked while committed entries remain unapplied, conservatively covering pending membership changes. Connection: support is evaluated in the current term and voter set, and prior commitment constrains later history; pending read support is abandoned on reset rather than carried into a new authority context. This is partial understanding, not a ready core map: membership application and recovery/completion ownership still need tracing.

Concrete source discrepancy retained for investigation: readIndex.confirm(ctx) returns every queued status through ctx, retaining each status's own ctx/from and assigning the confirming status's index; it removes all returned statuses from pending. handleReadIndexLeaderConfirmation uses s.ctx for local addReadyToRead, but its remote ReadIndexResp uses m.Hint/m.HintHigh (the confirming heartbeat context) for every returned status rather than s.ctx. A follower copies the received context into ReadyToRead, and pendingReadIndex.addReady updates only a batch with that exact SystemCtx. Thus a prefix containing distinct remote contexts has a sourced producer/consumer mismatch worth testing. No legal multi-request execution has yet been constructed, and no client timeout or consensus-safety violation has been measured.

Protection/counterevidence: batch completion remains gated by applied index; context generation chooses a nonzero random Low; duplicate same-context admission at the leader is ignored; unknown response senders are filtered at Peer.Handle; term transitions discard pending read support. Periodic heartbeat broadcasts target the latest pending read context, suggesting prefix release is an intended path rather than requiring arbitrary per-link response reordering. This needs a legal schedule and an exact identity-preservation obligation, not an invented global eventual-completion deadline. Source inspection also explains the initial apparent missing sender-membership check in candidate vote counting: the caller Peer.Handle provides it. Engine processing persists Raft state before ordinary post-save update handling, with explicitly separated early replication/fast-apply paths; their complete contract remains to be read.

after.meaning: The local entry log has a committed prefix through its committed index. Leader advancement by replica counting requires a quorum match at a current-term entry; follower and snapshot paths have distinct establishment conditions.

after.meaning: A queued readStatus binds an admitted context to its originating node and a captured committed index. Quorum confirmation releases the prefix through the confirmed context, retaining each original ctx/from while raising its index to the confirming status index. Release alone does not establish remote notification or application completion.
after.validity_context: Leader term-local pending queue; multi-voter admission follows current-term commitment. Authority reset discards pending statuses. Returned statuses exist synchronously for publication.
after.recovery: New authority creates an empty readIndex; caller timeout/drop handling is separate.

formation.explanation: The leader indexes proposals and aggregates per-voter/witness match acknowledgments into current-term commitment; followers validate the preceding term and protect the committed prefix. Commit propagates via replication and bounded heartbeats. Engine exports/persists state and queues committed entries to RSM, whose callbacks complete proposals and expose applied position. For reads, current-term commitment precedes distinct-voter heartbeat confirmation and prefix release; publication then feeds exact-context local batches, which additionally wait for application.

context.explanation: Election ticks campaign only for eligible nodes with no committed-but-unapplied entries. Available votes and up-to-date logs qualify support; known-peer response filtering and term dispatch precede aggregation. Higher terms, lost quorum and self-removal can remove authority; transfer waits for a full member to catch up and has a timeout. Reset discards pending read support and remote progress but preserves log commitment. New leadership appends a no-op and reconstructs pending config state. Membership changes are applied by the RSM then reflected in Raft under raftMu; recovery reconstructs snapshot membership and saved term/vote/log before later formation.

connection.explanation: Support is owned by the current term and installed membership. Authority transitions clear volatile votes/read support/progress, while persisted term/vote and protected committed history constrain future elections and replication. Applied membership updates redefine eligible participants and quorum; election blocking prevents campaigning before committed history is consumed. Confirmed reads bridge leadership support and client consumption through request context and application position, so release and notification are separate responsibilities. Stale-term replies are rejected; forwarded pending requests have distinct context, drop/timeout handling and no implicit completion guarantee from role acquisition.

Tick and authentic vote/replication messages establish term-2 leadership and index-4 commitment. Assertions check reached setup and admission. No test-only election override or state injection is used. Peer.ReadIndex generates the forwarded requests. Both first-context heartbeats are discarded by fixed policy; later messages retain generation order. Transport loss is permitted. Delaying replication until persistence strengthens setup ordering without excluding the overlapping reads. No crash or concurrent worker exists.

The release observation copies pending statuses before Peer.Handle of an authentic HeartbeatResp, then observes removal while still the same-term leader. Source inspection shows this path removes statuses through quorum prefix release, not reset/cancellation. Original status ctx/from is captured independently of replies. Events 5 and 6 establish release of two statuses with current-term commitment. Identity fields run/operation/request_node correlate results 7 and 8 independently of context, with one operation per distinct destination. The assertion compares complete decimal Low/High context content. Serialization also detects extra multiplicity, but the actual witness has exactly one reply and is a pure context mismatch; attribution does not require an extra exactly-once obligation. Policy applicability was fixed before execution. Release is the antecedent admitting this publication duty, not the compared result repeated as a prerequisite.

Raw output records setup term=2/committed=4, node 2 admission=101/1001 and node 3 admission=202/2002, then loss of both first-context heartbeats. Event 5 releases node 2 with expected_context=101/1001 on confirmation_context=202/2002. Result 7 has reply_count=1, reply_contexts=202/2002, ready_count=1, ready_contexts=202/2002, applied=4 and term=2. Event 6/result 8 preserve node 3 context=202/2002. These agree with retained controller correlations, one violating witness and no parse errors. Replies are copied from actual generated messages; readiness is copied from GetUpdate before Commit clears it. All copies, protocol calls and policy state belong to the synchronous test goroutine. Results follow full message queue drain and update completion. completed=true denotes that finite driver endpoint, not NodeHost RequestCompleted. The constructors create synchronous peers and in-memory storage, so there is no worker/join/Close duty omitted. Exit code is zero; test success indicates process completion only. The observed mismatch is explained by remote publication selecting m.Hint/m.HintHigh instead of s.ctx. No client timeout or global safety inference is necessary for this local discrepancy.

Explained alternatives and limits: The later request receives its correct 202/2002 context in the same execution. Local release uses s.ctx, and sequential safe-read tests preserve context; this finding concerns earlier remote statuses in a prefix. Current-term commitment, membership response filtering and application gating remain present but do not repair emitted identity.
items.report_title: 批量确认读取时，较早请求被回填为较晚请求的上下文
items.report_answer: 节点 2 的请求上下文为 101/1001，但后续确认释放两个请求时，其回复与可读通知均携带节点 3 的 202/2002；节点 3 的回复正确。该执行支持稳定成员、同一任期下的请求关联缺陷，未测量客户端超时或更广泛的一致性后果。
limitations: Package-level no-crash execution with synchronous storage/application/transport substitutes; no NodeHost client-timeout measurement.
Follower readiness is diagnostic; the formal predicate compares reply context.
No cluster-wide linearizability or eventual-progress verdict.
